newsitem.title: FRANCE: TENNIS-'BAD BOY' INSISTS IT TAKES TWO TO TARANGO.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-'BAD BOY' INSISTS IT TAKES TWO TO TARANGO.

text.p: Volatile American Jeff Tarango's antics during his second round French Open match against Thomas Muster will not impress the authorities at Wimbledon as they prepare to receive him back to the All England Club next month.

Tarango has yet to confirm whether he plans to play at Wimbledon, but knows he is still a marked man after being suspended and hit with a record fine in 1995 when he walked off court during his third round match against German Alexander Mronz.

Accusing French referee Bruno Rebeuh of being "the most corrupt official in the game" -- an allegation later retracted -- earned him censure from all sides, yet he shows no signs of adopting a lower profile.
While Tarango completed his match this time, losing in four sets to the 1995 French champion on Wednesday, it did not end amicably.
The two men, at times acting more like the school children packed into the stands for Kids Day at Roland Garros, engaged in an ill-tempered affair littered with name-calling, mimicking and taunts.
It ended with the Austrian refusing to shake Tarango's hand amid deafening boos and whistles.

"If the media wants to make me the bad boy, they can do that," said Tarango, a nine-year journeyman professional still searching for his first career tournament win. "But I think if you come and watch my matches you will not get that impression.
"My reputation precedes me a little bit, but I think it's a bit of a false reputation."
Over the years, Muster hasn't exactly ingratiated himself as a friend of Wimbledon either.
He has regularly refused to play there and said last year he planned to tear up all the grass at his home and replace it with asphalt.
Tarango's behaviour, however, left him even less impressed.

"There's no excuse for certain behaviour on the court," argued Muster, not always a model of decorum on the court himself. "I know I'm not always great but when I'm on the court I'm fighting, I'm giving everything, I'm looking at balls and ball marks.
"But that's all within the rules. I don't think what we saw today was very professional
"It's not right that you're playing a match and you can do anything you want, then at the end everyone smiles and shakes hands. That's not the way it works."
Hopefully, things will be calmer on Thursday when top games include number two seed Michael Chang against Jerome Golmard of France and Martina Hingis against Italy's Gloria Pizzichini.
